title: Strings
description: Storing text, joining it together, and why numbers need converting before they join.

parts.label: type
parts.note: Text of any length: a word, a sentence, or nothing at all.

parts.label: value
parts.note: Text always goes in double quotes.

content.title: Anatomy of a string variable
content.caption: Declared exactly like the other types.
To use `string`, add `#include <string>` next to `#include <iostream>`.

content.value: `string` is not a fundamental type. It is a **class**: a type built from simpler pieces and shipped in the standard library. Its full name is `std::string`.
Some programs seem to work without `#include <string>`, because `iostream` happens to pull it in on that compiler. Do not rely on luck.
content.title: Always include it

content.value: `+` joins strings, left to right. C++ adds nothing of its own, so every space must be inside the quotes.

steps.note: Joined with no space between them.
The `" "` in the middle adds the space.
The joined text is new text. Store it in its own variable.
Use the stored result like any other string.

content.title: Joining step by step

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `+` joins the pieces in order and adds no spaces of its own.
content.code:
string a = "Hi";
cout << a + "!" + a << endl;

content.value: Two Quoted Pieces Will Not Join
A C++ quirk: quoted text on its own is not a `string` yet. It is an older kind of text from C. Two of those cannot be joined with `+`.

items.title: Error
items.text: Both sides of the first `+` are quoted text.

items.title: Compiles
items.text: It starts with a real `string`, so every later `+` makes a `string` too.

content.title: Where the chain starts matters
content.caption: If the compiler complains about `invalid operands` to `+`, this is almost always why.

content.question: Which line is an error?
content.explain: The first `+` joins two quoted pieces. Every other line starts its chain with the `string` variable `name`.

content.value: Inside `cout` you never need `+` to mix numbers and text: `<<` prints each piece in turn. `+` is worked out before `<<`, so a sum in the chain is maths.

content.caption: Line two sends 2 then 3 with nothing between. Two numbers stuck together? A missing space or `+` is the reason.

items.title: Nonsense
items.text: Compiles, but joins nothing. It gives garbage or crashes.

items.title: Works
items.text: `to_string` turns the number into text first.

content.title: Joining a number into a string
content.caption: Printing? Use `<<` and mix anything. Building a `string` to keep? Use `+` and wrap numbers in `to_string`.

parts.label: dot
parts.note: Means: ask this value to do something. Classes can do things as well as hold a value.

parts.label: do it now
parts.note: The empty brackets run the action.

content.title: Asking a string a question
content.caption: `size()` does exactly the same job as `length()`.
Strings can find words, cut out pieces and more. Module 7 covers the ones worth knowing.

items.title: char
items.text: Single quotes. Exactly one character, like a grade or a menu key.

items.title: string
items.text: Double quotes. Any amount of text, even one character or none.

content.title: char vs string
content.caption: They print the same, which is exactly why mixing them up confuses people.

content.question: Which line is an error?
content.explain: Double quotes make text, and text cannot squeeze into a `char` box.

practice.question: Declare a `string` for your town and one for your country, then print them as one line: Town, Country.
Build a `string` called `message` that holds Level 5 unlocked, using `+` and `to_string` on an `int` variable called `level`. Then print `message`.
Store your full name in a `string`, then print a line saying how many characters it has, including the space.

quiz.question: What must you add at the top of a program that uses `string`?
options: Nothing: string is a fundamental type.
quiz.explain: `string` comes from the standard library, so you include its header, just as `<iostream>` brings in `cout`.

quiz.question: What does `cout << "Sum: " << 2 + 3 << endl;` print?
quiz.explain: `+` is worked out before `<<`, so `2 + 3` becomes 5 and then 5 is printed.

quiz.question: What does `string s = "Score: " + to_string(7);` store?
quiz.explain: `to_string` turns the number 7 into the text "7", and `+` joins it onto the end of "Score: ".

quiz.question: If `string word = "C++";`, what does `word.length()` give back?
quiz.explain: `length()` counts the characters in the text, and `+` signs are characters too. Spaces count as well.

quiz.question: Which line is correct?
quiz.explain: A `string` value needs double quotes. Single quotes make a `char`, and C++ will not quietly swap one for the other here.
